Where Archie fits

Set up Archie for your email and calendar.

Five steps, no code

Install Archie, choose your AI account and connect your chat. See the five stepsSource 1.

Your agent on your computer

Your agent and memory live on your computer. Your words go to your chosen AI company by defaultSource 1.

AI on your computer must pass a check that it can use tools. Connected services and web requests still leave your computerSource 1.

Replies and calendar changes need your yes

Replies and calendar changes wait for your approval. No setting turns that asking offSource 1.

Personal is free at 20 jobs a day on your own AI account; paid plans start at $30 a month plus AI usageSource 1.

When a Personal plan ends, existing agents keep working at 20 jobs a day on your own AI account. Your files remain; check what changes.

The alternatives

Four ways to get help from AI.

Choose by the job, where the agent runs, and how much setup you want.

Checked October 1, 2026. Monthly US prices; AI usage and limits differ.

Hosted agents

Lindy, alfred_ and Martin

Lindy handles inboxes and workflows: $29.99 per userSource 12. alfred_ handles email, calendars and tasks: $29.99Source 13. Reach Martin by text, calls, email or SlackSource 14.

alfred_ stores your email and memory on its infrastructureSource 13. Lindy and alfred_ also require approval for email sendsSource 12Source 13.

AI subscriptions

ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini

ChatGPT offers chat, research and agent featuresSource 19. Claude Pro is $20 a monthSource 15, and Google AI Pro, which includes Gemini, is $19.99 a monthSource 16.

Agent features vary by plan. These subscriptions do not pay for Archie’s separate AI usageSource 1.

Scheduling and work planners

Motion and Reclaim

Reclaim focuses on your calendar, scheduling tasks, habits and meetingsSource 18. Motion also covers projects, documents, notes and workflowsSource 17.

A planner may fit best if scheduling is the job you want handled.

Open-source agents

OpenClaw and your own build

OpenClaw runs on your computer, supports local models and has no software subscriptionSource 3. AI and hosting costs are separate.

Its code is open, and it offers desktop setup tooSource 3. Compare OpenClaw’s controls with Archie’s, or bring an OpenClaw agent over.

See the detailed comparison of eleven agents
Eleven agents, two questions

Of eleven agents, only Archie works on your own computer and asks first, with no off switch.

Every agent we could source

Eleven agents, placed from what their own pages say.

The same eleven on two axes, every placement sourced below. Across is whose computer the work happens on. Up is your pick: asks first is what a product does before a step that matters, and ease is how you get it running.

The top right is the corner we are aiming at, and in the Ease view nobody has reached it, us included. Read September 18, 2026, and September 30 for OpenAI Dots.

Where the other ten win

Five things they do that Archie does not.

Open source

Hermes, OpenClaw and Vellum publish their code, so you can read every line and change what you likeSource 2Source 3Source 4. Archie’s is not published; you can watch every connection it makes, and our Trust page shows you how. New tools come in our releases, or from a service you connect (MCP). Why Archie’s code is not published →

The most control on the board

OpenClaw has five permission modes, one that asks before every command, and allow lists per commandSource 3. Archie’s asking is built in: less to set up, and less to change.

Working while everything you own is off

OpenAI Dots, a Grok Bot and Symphony’s agents keep going with your laptop shutSource 11Source 6Source 8. Archie answers only while your computer is awake, though it can wake it for a routine set for a time. What to leave on is on How It Works.

A free plan with the AI included

Symphony’s free plan comes with AI credits that reset every monthSource 8, and Muse is “free for most of what people need”Source 7. Archie is free on an AI account of your own at 20 jobs a day, and you pay that company for what you use.

A phone app in the app stores

Symphony, Muse and Vellum each have one in the storesSource 8Source 7Source 2. Archie Mobile installs on Android from a file today, and the iPhone app is with Apple for review.

Sources for every placement and claim on this page
1Archie: whose computer, what it asks, and how you get it

Our own Trust page sets out where the work happens and each gate named at the top of this page. It lists everything Archie sends and to whom, and shows how to watch it yourself with a network monitor. Archie is a download from our install page, which is the app row.

The overview was checked October 1, 2026 against our five-step walkthrough, pricing page and cancellation terms. The Trust page covers local model checks and the requests that still leave your computer. A paid plan grants app access; keeping your agent’s files does not mean paid access continues after cancellation.

2Vellum: runs locally by default, and asks until you change a setting

Read from vellum.ai on September 16, 2026. “By default, your assistant runs locally.” And: “High-stakes actions like sending emails to new contacts, modifying important files, or spending credits require explicit approval until you mark them as trusted.”

Its permissions docs, read September 18, give four modes, from Strict, “Everything: every action requires explicit approval”, to Full access, “your assistant never asks for permission”, which is why asking is a setting there.

Its download page, read September 18, offers “Vellum for Mac: Native Mac app with computer use” and “Vellum for Windows: Desktop app for Windows PCs”, which is the app row. It also lists the App Store and Google Play, and the homepage says Vellum is open source.

Its pricing page, read September 16, says “Vellum is free to download and start.”

3OpenClaw: on your computer, free, and acting on its own by default

Read from openclaw.ai on September 16, 2026. “Mac, Windows, or Linux. Bring hosted, subscription-backed, gateway, or local models. State lives on your machine, not a vendor cloud.” It says it has no subscription, no hosted tier and no token, and it is MIT licensed.

Its docs on tool and agent permissions, read the same day, say: “Full Access, including Default (Full Access), authorizes permitted changes without an approval prompt; restricted runs require human approval”. So by default it acts on its own, and you can make it ask.

Read again September 18: its exec approvals give five modes, “deny”, “allowlist”, “ask”, “auto” and “full”, an “ask: always” that “keeps prompting”, and per-command allow lists, which is the most control on this board. Its getting-started is a shell command, “Try it in one command”, which is the terminal row; openclaw.ai also offers “Desktop Apps: Full apps that install everything for you”.

Homepage re-read October 1, 2026 for the overview: on-computer storage, local models, open source, no subscription and desktop setup are still listed. The overview includes desktop setup rather than describing OpenClaw as requiring code for every installation.

4Hermes: a desktop app, free and MIT, and asking by default

Read from hermes-agent.nousresearch.com on September 16, 2026, the Nous Research page for it. It leads with a desktop app for macOS and Windows, which is the app row, and adds a terminal install that also covers Linux and “Deploy to the cloud” through Nous Portal. It is “free and open source under the MIT license”.

Its security docs, read the same day: “Before executing any command, Hermes checks it against a curated list of dangerous patterns. If a match is found, the user must explicitly approve it”, with three modes, “smart | manual | off”, which is why asking your permission is a setting there.

5Claude Cowork: Anthropic’s servers, and a mode that does not ask

Read from Anthropic’s Cowork guide on August 20, 2026. “Open Claude on the web at claude.ai, in the Claude Desktop app, or in the Claude mobile app”, choose Cowork, and “describe the task you want Claude to complete”, which is the sign-in row. Cowork’s work “runs on Anthropic’s servers, in an isolated environment, and your sessions and files are saved to your Claude account”.

Re-read September 16, 2026: the mode selector “offers Auto and Manual (default)”, and in Manual “Claude pauses and asks for approval for actions”. In Skip mode, “Claude doesn’t pause to ask and nothing checks its actions automatically”.

6Grok Bot: a persistent cloud VM, and it comes back for your approval

Read from x.ai/news/introducing-grok-bot and the Grok Bot overview on August 20, 2026, and again September 16. Each Grok Bot “runs on a persistent cloud VM with a browser, filesystem, and terminal”, and “They finish jobs end to end, and only come back when something needs your approval”.

That is why it sits at the top with Symphony and Norton. The same page says “Download the app, create your first teammate, and start handing off work”, with a Download for macOS button, which is the app row.

7Meta Muse: a dedicated cloud computer, free for most

Read from Meta’s announcement on September 15, 2026. Muse “runs on its own dedicated computer in the cloud, contained so no one else’s agent can reach it”. It is “free for most of what people need, with subscription plans for people who want to do more”. It is “rolling out in the US on iOS, Android, and muse.ai”, which is the sign-in row.

Its permissions, read September 18 and again September 28, are one of two settings: “Always ask”, or “Ask for some actions”, which asks “before every write action and important read actions”. When it asks, it offers “Always allow”, which lets it take “this type of action for this Connector in the future without asking again”. That is why Muse sits a short way below the top, beside Cowork.

8Wix Symphony: how you reach it, and where the work happens

Read from wix.com/symphony on September 11, 2026. Symphony is used with a Wix account, in a browser or its iOS and Android apps, and Wix publishes no program you run on your own computer, which is the sign-in row. Wix’s overview says it “checks with you first before your agents act, so nothing important happens without your approval”.

Read again September 18: “Your agents connect to the suite of tools you already use and can work on their own, 24/7”, and “your agents’ background work uses AI credits”. Wix publishes no sentence saying where that work runs.

Symphony’s agents work while you are away, and Wix ships only a phone app and a browser, so we place Symphony on the their-servers side. That placement is our reading of those two sentences, and if Wix publishes the sentence either way we will cite it.

Its pricing page, read September 11: a free plan, “no credit card needed”, whose credits “reset monthly”.

9Instinct: in private access, hosted, and acting on its own

Read from instinct.com on September 16, 2026. “Text Instinct to get started”: nothing is installed, which is the sign-in row, and it is “currently available to a private access group as we’re scaling up compute”. Its privacy policy, read the same day, places it: the service is provided with “third-party hosting”, and its features “can perform tasks or take actions independently on your behalf, based on the permissions you grant”.

10Norton Family Assistant: asks first, and runs in the cloud

Read from us.norton.com/products/family-assistant on September 16, 2026: “Asks first, acts after”. Its support FAQ, read September 18, 2026, says where it runs: “your family graph, connected-account tokens, agent context, and chat history all live inside your own dedicated instance in the cloud, isolated from other users”.

That is why it sits on the their-servers side. It “works on any PCs that run in browsers such as Norton Neo, Chrome, and Firefox” or as an iPhone app, which is the sign-in row.

11OpenAI Dots: a cloud computer of its own, asking by rules you can change

OpenAI’s announcement, read September 30, 2026, says each dot “works on its own cloud computer, while your computer and its contents stay separate unless you choose to connect it”. Its help center says access to your own computer “is optional and starts turned off”, and ChatGPT’s guide that a dot “can keep working even when your computer is off”. That is why it sits on the their-servers side.

The same announcement says dots “start with built-in rules for when to act independently and when to ask for approval”. One rule you can add, on its controls page, is “Take action without asking”, which is why it sits a short way below the top, beside Cowork and Muse.

“Create your dot in the ChatGPT desktop app or in ChatGPT on desktop web”, which is the sign-in row. It comes with ChatGPT Pro and Business Premium. OpenAI’s pages refuse scripts, so we read them through a service that returns a page’s own text.

12Lindy: price, inbox work and approvals

Lindy’s pricing page, read October 1, 2026, lists Plus at $29.99 per user a month, inbox management and scheduled routines. It also lists thousands of integrations. Its FAQ says actions with outside impact, including sending email, wait for approval.

13alfred_: price, stored content and email approval

Its plan documentation, read October 1, 2026, lists one $29.99 monthly plan including email, calendars and tasks. Its privacy documentation names email content, memory and conversation history stored on US infrastructure, including Supabase. Its FAQ says drafts wait for review and Send.

14Martin: ways to reach the service

Martin’s homepage, read October 1, 2026, offers text, calls, email and Slack, along with calendar scheduling and email drafts. No Martin price is used in this overview.

15Claude: the monthly Pro price

Anthropic’s pricing page, read October 1, 2026, lists Claude Pro at $20 billed monthly. The annual discount is a different billing choice.

16Google AI Pro: Gemini and the US monthly price

Google’s US plan page, read October 1, 2026, lists Google AI Pro at $19.99 a month and includes expanded Gemini access. Regional availability and limits vary.

17Motion: work tools beyond calendars

Motion’s homepage, read October 1, 2026, lists projects, tasks, calendars, meetings, documents, notes, reports and workflows. Calling it only a calendar tool would omit these products.

18Reclaim: calendar scheduling

Reclaim’s homepage, read October 1, 2026, presents an AI calendar with scheduling for tasks, habits, focus time and meetings. No claim about being cheaper than Archie is made here.

19ChatGPT: features vary by plan

OpenAI’s pricing page, read October 1, 2026, lists chat and deep research, with its always-on Dot agent on Pro. Agent features differ by plan.
